about.heading: About Me
about.p1: As a Game Developer, my passion lies in creating immersive experiences where game mechanics and narrative organically intertwine. My goal is for every interaction to be so intuitive that players grasp it naturally, allowing the emotion and intention behind the creation to be fully felt.
about.p2: Beyond the technical aspects of game development, I am a storytelling enthusiast, dedicated to crafting engaging narratives, whether for personal exploration or as potential foundations for new game worlds. My curiosity leads me to be an avid reader, exploring everything from philosophy and history to fiction and science. I'm particularly fascinated by astrophysics, unraveling the mysteries of the universe, and I love spending time with my dogs. In my leisure time, I'm an eclectic gamer, with a special fondness for indie games, which I consider true gems in terms of innovation and creativity.
about.p3: I'm seeking new opportunities to contribute to innovative projects, where my passion for creating games I'd love to play can flourish. My differential is the ability to simplify processes and act as a facilitator, always considering how my contributions can optimize teamwork and solve complex challenges. I'm a natural problem-solver and I love to refine every detail to ensure the best possible experience.
about.creative: Before focusing my career on game development, I worked for years in creative fields that provided me with a robust visual foundation, including work with photography in analog labs, as a video editor, and as a newspaper layout designer. This background allows me to have a 360-degree view of the final product, integrating the technical aspects of programming with high aesthetic and narrative quality.

vrTennis.desc: Meta Quest 2 game focused on realistic racket physics and immersive, spin-enabled ball behavior using multi-point collision and Magnus effect.
vrTennis.h1: Technical Analysis: TennisVR - Realistic Physics for Meta Quest 2
vrTennis.p1: TennisVR is a Meta Quest 2 project that pushes the limits of physics simulation to create an authentic virtual tennis experience. The main goal was to replicate the feel and control of a real racket, allowing players to perform everything from simple hits to complex shots like topspins and slices naturally.
vrTennis.h2: The Challenge: Realistic Racket Impact in VR
vrTennis.p2: The biggest challenge in any VR sports game involving striking an object is physics. A single collider on the racket cannot capture the nuances of a real hit. It doesn't matter if the player hits the ball with the tip or the sweet spot; the resulting speed would tend to be the same, depending only on overall controller velocity. This breaks immersion because an experienced player expects the tip of the racket, moving in an arc, to be much faster than the handle.
vrTennis.p3: To solve this, I implemented a technique that simulates multiple contact points on the racket. Instead of a single collider, the racket surface was equipped with a grid of invisible follower capsules, each with its own Rigidbody and Collider.
vrTennis.p4: These capsules are not part of the racket itself but follow it in real time. In FixedUpdate(), each capsule calculates the velocity needed to reach its corresponding point on the racket. As a result, capsules at the extremity move faster than those near the grip, simulating the swing arc. The tennis ball collides only with these capsules, ensuring the impact point precisely determines rebound velocity and direction.
vrTennis.h4: Solution 2: Adding Spin with the Magnus Effect
vrTennis.p5: A tennis shot is not just about speed; spin is fundamental. To simulate topspin and slice effects, I implemented the Magnus Effect. At impact, the system calculates the angular velocity (spin) applied to the ball based on the racket's speed and angle. During flight, a continuous force is applied to its Rigidbody, perpendicular to its movement direction and spin axis, producing an authentic trajectory.
vrTennis.p6: The combination of these techniques resulted in an intuitive and physically accurate VR tennis experience. The project demonstrates proficiency in advanced physics simulation, VR gameplay, and translating real-world phenomena into interactive mechanics in Unity.

intro.title: Technical Analysis: WaterPuzzle - Shader-Driven Physics in Godot
intro.p1: WaterPuzzle is a mobile puzzle game developed in Godot 4, where players must organize colored liquids by pouring them between cans until each container holds only one pure color. The project showcases advanced shader programming, spring physics simulation, and procedural puzzle generation without relying on heavy 3D physics engines.
intro.p2: This project demonstrates mastery in GLSL shader programming, physics simulation, procedural generation, and performance optimization for mobile platforms. The entire liquid behavior—from surface waves to inertia—is achieved through custom shaders and spring physics, resulting in realistic visuals at minimal performance cost.

challenge.title: The Challenge: Realistic Liquid Without 3D Physics
challenge.p1: Simulating realistic liquid behavior is computationally expensive. Traditional approaches using particle systems or fluid dynamics are prohibitive for mobile devices. The challenge was to create convincing liquid physics—including surface tension, wave propagation, inertia, and multi-colored layering—using only 2D shaders and mathematical models.
challenge.p2: Additionally, the game needed to support dynamic difficulty levels with varying can capacities (3-8 units), multiple liquid colors with distinct visual properties, smooth pour animations with realistic timing, and maintain 60 FPS on mid-range mobile devices.

shader.title: Solution 1: Multi-Layer Liquid Shader with Surface Physics
shader.p1: The core innovation is a custom GLSL shader (liquid_lab.gdshader) that renders up to 8 distinct liquid layers with individual colors, realistic surface behavior, and advanced visual effects. The shader operates entirely in UV space, transforming coordinates based on the can's tilt angle to simulate gravity.
shader.li1: Gravity-Based UV Transformation: Uses a rotation matrix to align the liquid surface with the gravitational vector, making the liquid always "level" regardless of can orientation.
shader.li2: Multi-Layer System: Supports up to 8 color layers with smooth blending between boundaries. Each layer has configurable blend amounts for vertical and horizontal transitions.
shader.li3: Meniscus Effect: Simulates surface curvature near the can walls using pow(abs(x_offset), 3.0) for physically accurate concave/convex shapes.
shader.li4: Wave Propagation: Sine-based wave generation with configurable frequency and amplitude, synchronized with game time.
shader.li5: Sloshing Simulation: Horizontal oscillation using phase-shifted sine waves to simulate liquid momentum during pour animations.
shader.li6: Rim Lighting: Edge detection using mask alpha gradients to create realistic highlights at liquid boundaries.
shader.caption: Shader breakdown showing gravity-aligned UV transformation and multi-layer rendering

physics.title: Solution 2: Spring Physics for Liquid Inertia
physics.p1: To complement the shader, I implemented a spring-damper system in GDScript that simulates liquid inertia and surface oscillation. This creates natural-looking "lag" when the can rotates, making the liquid feel like it has mass and momentum.
physics.li1: Surface Angle Physics: Spring system with configurable stiffness (18.0) and damping (7.5) that makes the liquid surface gradually align with gravity.
physics.li2: Surface Offset: Lateral displacement based on angular velocity, simulating liquid "sloshing" to one side during rotation.
physics.li3: Adaptive Damping: Higher damping when vertical (0.88) to reduce oscillation at rest, lower when tilted (0.94) for more dynamic movement.
physics.li4: Per-Liquid Profiles: Different wave, meniscus, and highlight multipliers for each color type (e.g., water is wavier, syrup has stronger meniscus).
physics.caption: Spring physics creating natural inertia and surface oscillation

pour.title: Solution 3: Optimized Pour Animation System
pour.p1: The pour animation is the most complex interaction, involving three phases: approach (rotating the source can), transfer (liquid flowing out and in), and return (can rotation back to rest). The challenge was making this feel natural while maintaining responsiveness.
pour.p2: I implemented an overlapping animation system that starts the liquid transfer 0.4 seconds before the rotation completes. This creates a more fluid visual experience and reduces total animation time from ~2.8s to ~2.0s—a 28% improvement in responsiveness.
pour.p3: The liquid stream connecting cans is implemented using dynamically positioned ColorRect nodes that animate their height and alpha. When the stream reaches the destination surface, a particle system creates a splash effect with physics-based particle velocities.
pour.caption: Three-phase pour animation with overlapping timing optimization

generation.title: Solution 4: Procedural Puzzle Generation & Validation
generation.p1: Puzzles are generated using a reverse-solve algorithm: start from the solved state (each color in its own can) and apply random valid moves to shuffle. This guarantees every puzzle is solvable. A separate validation system verifies solution integrity and detects impossible states.
generation.li1: Difficulty Levels: Support for 3-8 unit capacities with increasing complexity.
generation.li2: State Validation: Real-time checks ensure conservation of liquid units and color counts.
generation.li3: Undo/Redo System: Full state history with deep copy to prevent reference bugs.
generation.li4: Solution Tracking: Debug system displays optimal solution path for testing.

architecture.title: Software Architecture & Design Patterns
architecture.p1: The project employs several software engineering best practices:
architecture.li1: State Machine Pattern: Pour animations managed as explicit states (idle → animating → committing) to prevent race conditions.
architecture.li2: Singleton Autoloads: PuzzleLogic and SolutionValidator provide centralized game rules and validation.
architecture.li3: Observer Pattern: Group notifications (add_to_group("first_screen")) for decoupled difficulty changes.
architecture.li4: Component-Based Design: Can class is fully self-contained with its own shader, physics, and animation logic.
architecture.li5: Separation of Concerns: Visual staging (shader animations) separated from logical commits (state changes).
